title: Memory order
text: Pattern eleven: memory order. Two threads share a ring, and every atomic operation picks an ordering. The default is the strongest, and on x86, one of its stores is a full barrier.

title: The general version
text: Here is the general version: an SPSC ring where every load and store uses the default ordering. Call load or store with no argument, and you get sequential consistency. It is correct, and the easiest model to reason about. But this protocol never needed it: each index has one writer, and it only passes messages.

title: x86-TSO
text: x86 already orders memory strongly. Under its TSO model, loads stay in order with loads, and stores stay in order with stores. But stores wait in a per-core store buffer, so a later load can pass an earlier store. That is the one reordering seq_cst must forbid. So a seq_cst load is a plain mov. A seq_cst store becomes xchg, a locked instruction that drains the store buffer before the core moves on.

title: The hot-path version
text: On the right, the same ring, with only the orderings it needs. The owner reads its own index relaxed. The other side reads it with acquire. The owner publishes with release. That pair makes the slot write happen before the consumer's read of it.

title: The generated code
text: Now compile both with g++ -O2, and look at push. Every instruction matches, except one: xchg on the left, mov on the right. The loads are the same mov in both. Pop is the same story, with one xchg on the tail.

title: Not free everywhere
text: So is release free? On x86, at the instruction level, yes. But it still binds the compiler: no slot write may sink below the release store. On ARM, acquire and release are real instructions, ldar and stlr. There, a seq_cst store is the same stlr, so the big gap is an x86 story.

title: Measured
text: Measured on a shared 4-vCPU cloud VM. In a one-thread publish loop, a seq_cst publish took 11.6 nanoseconds, and a release publish 2.5. That is 4.6 times. Through the ring, with two pinned threads, it was 164 nanoseconds per message against 48, median of five runs. One seq_cst run matched release, so the gap depends on timing. When the slot store misses in cache, the barrier waits for that miss.

title: The honest nuance
text: Seq_cst is the right default when you are unsure, and some protocols need one total order, like Dekker-style flags. The bloat comes from a missing statement: one writer per index, message passing only. Say that, and acquire and release are enough. Rule: on x86, a seq_cst store is a full barrier. Publish with release, and read with acquire.
